core: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy (NASA, OpenStax)
Structure: flat rotating disk, central bulge, and spherical halo
Sun located in the disk about 26,000 light-years from the galactic center, roughly halfway out
Galactic center hosts Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole of about 4 million solar masses
The night-sky Milky Way band is the disk of our own galaxy seen edge-on from inside
supporting: Roughly 100 billion stars in the Milky Way (estimate)
Solar system orbits the galactic center about once every 240 million years (NASA)
The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group of more than 50 galaxies
Star-orbit observations at the center won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics

claims.claim: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy: a flat, rotating disk whose spiral arms wind off the ends of a central bar of older stars.
The Milky Way's disk of stars spans about 100,000 light-years in diameter.

The galaxy's visible structure has three named parts: the thin rotating disk, a central bulge of mostly older stars within about 10,000 light-years of the center, and a spherical halo of very old, faint stars extending at least 150,000 light-years from the center.
The Sun lies inside the disk, about 26,000 light-years from the galactic center, roughly halfway from the center to the disk's edge, on a small arm called the Orion Arm (Orion Spur).

At the galactic center sits Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole with a mass of about 4 million Suns (OpenStax cites about 4.6 million), detected through radio emission and the orbits of stars around it.
The pale band of the Milky Way across the night sky is the central disk of our own galaxy seen edge-on from inside the disk.
The Milky Way is one galaxy among billions; it belongs to the Local Group of more than 50 galaxies, whose nearest large member is Andromeda.
The solar system takes about 240 million years to orbit the Milky Way once (NASA GSFC's estimate is about 250 million years).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Number of spiral arms: older descriptions give the Milky Way four major arms; the current consensus describes two major arms wrapping off a central bar.
positions: NASA GSFC Imagine the Universe page (older, no longer updated) describes four spiral arms.

NASA's Spitzer-based resource (2017) and current science.nasa.gov pages describe two major arms (Scutum-Centaurus, Perseus) attached to a central bar, with two thinner minor arms (Norma, Sagittarius) between them.
OpenStax Astronomy 2e describes a central bar with two main spiral arms connecting to its ends.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson uses the current consensus: barred spiral galaxy with two major arms off a central bar, and the Sun near the small Orion Spur. The older four-arm description is noted in the source record but not taught.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Mass of Sagittarius A*: NASA gives about 4 million solar masses; OpenStax gives about 4.6 million solar masses.
positions: NASA Science Black Holes overview: '4 million times the Sun's mass.'
OpenStax Astronomy 2e 25.4: 'a black hole with a mass equivalent to 4.6 million Suns.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson states 'about 4 million solar masses' (NASA figure) and notes the range; both sources agree it is a supermassive black hole.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sun's distance from the galactic center: NASA GSFC gives about 25,000 light-years; OpenStax gives about 26,000 light-years.
positions: NASA Imagine the Universe: 'about 25,000 light years away from the center.'
OpenStax Astronomy 2e 25.3: 'the Sun orbits that point from a distance of about 26,000 light-years.'
NASA science.nasa.gov galaxies page describes Earth as 'about halfway from the center.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson uses 'about 26,000 light-years' (OpenStax, matching the task's checked figure) and 'about halfway out' (NASA); both figures are about 8 kiloparsecs (1 kpc = 3,260 light-years per OpenStax).

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's boilerplate ('Milky Way is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.') contains no factual content and was fully replaced.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate draft with source-verified content from NASA and OpenStax.
Taught the current two-major-arm barred-spiral description rather than the older four-arm picture.
Stated the Sun's location explicitly (about 26,000 light-years from the center, in the disk, about halfway out) instead of leaving it vague.
Kept galaxy types, stars, universe, and solar-system content out of scope per sibling-topic boundaries.
rightsIssues: None. All sources are reference-only (NASA public-domain government pages; OpenStax CC BY 4.0 open textbook); no source prose, figures, or tables reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Galaxies: Overview (Galaxy Basics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports: the Milky Way as our home galaxy; a spiral galaxy with a disk of stars spanning more than 100,000 light-years; Earth located along one of the galaxy's spiral arms about halfway from the center; the solar system's ~240-million-year orbit of the Milky Way; the Milky Way band as the central disk seen edge-on; and the Local Group of more than 50 galaxies with Andromeda as the nearest large member. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: The Milky Way Galaxy (artist's concept)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). NASA resource page (November 2017) based on Spitzer Space Telescope infrared surveys. Supports: the Milky Way's barred spiral structure, with two major arms (Scutum-Centaurus and Perseus) attached to the ends of a thick central bar and two thinner minor arms (Norma and Sagittarius) between them; and the Sun lying near a small partial arm, the Orion Arm (Orion Spur), between the Sagittarius and Perseus arms. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Black Holes (Overview)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports: Sagittarius A* as the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, about 4 million times the Sun's mass; the tracking of star orbits near the galactic center as the proof of the supermassive black hole, a discovery that won the 2020 Nobel Prize; and the statement that most Milky Way-sized galaxies have central supermassive black holes. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: The Milky Way Galaxy (Imagine the Universe)
sourceRecords.provider: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (Imagine the Universe)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Older NASA education page (site carries a 'lapse in federal government funding' notice and is no longer updated). Supports: the Milky Way as a large barred spiral galaxy; an estimate of roughly 100 billion stars; a disk diameter of about 100,000 light-years; the Sun about 25,000 light-years from the center; the ~250-million-year solar orbit; and the band of the Milky Way as the disk seen from inside. Its four-arm description conflicts with the current two-major-arm consensus and is NOT used; the current view is taught instead.

sourceRecords.title: Astronomy 2e, Section 25.1 The Architecture of the Galaxy
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports: the thin, circular, rotating disk about 100,000 light-years in diameter and about 2,000 light-years thick; the central bulge (nuclear bulge) forming within about 10,000 light-years of the center; the spherical halo of very old, faint stars extending at least 150,000 light-years from the center; the barred-structure evidence (central bar of old yellow-red stars with two main spiral arms connecting to its ends); and the Sun on the inside edge of the short Orion spur. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Astronomy 2e, Section 25.3 The Mass of the Galaxy
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports: the Sun orbiting the galactic center from a distance of about 26,000 light-years; the definition of a kiloparsec as 3,260 light-years (so ~26,000 light-years is about 8 kiloparsecs); and the Milky Way's mass of about 100 billion solar masses derived via Kepler's third law. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Astronomy 2e, Section 25.4 The Center of the Galaxy
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports: Sagittarius A* as the bright radio source in the nucleus of the galaxy; evidence that the very center contains a supermassive black hole with a mass equivalent to about 4.6 million Suns confined within less than the diameter of Mercury's orbit; and the definition of supermassive black holes as central masses far greater than stellar-mass black holes. Reference only; prose synthesized.
